newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian firms warn of negative economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian firms warn of negative economic growth.

text.p: Nigeria's manufacturers on Friday warned that economic growth in 1997 will be negative unless the military government changes its policies to stimulate demand.

Uzor Okeke, director general of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria said policies aimed at keeping inflation low and the naira currency strong were forcing factories out of business and deepening recession.
"If the situation does not change then there will definitely be negative growth this year," Okeke told Reuters in an interview.

GDP growth was 3.25 percent in 1996 compared with 2.20 percent in 1995, according to government figures. But in June the central bank said first quarter 1997 economic performance was mixed and that the "real sector" of the economy remained weak.
"The squeeze on liquidity combined with the late release of the capital votes (spending) have had the effect of depriving Nigerians of any spending power," Okeke said.
"Unemployment is high and rising and factories are producing goods which end up destined only for the warehouses because nobody can buy," he added.
Low inflation and a stable naira currency are the goals which military ruler General Sani Abacha, his finance ministry and central bank, have pursued with both vigour and success.
Inflation in May was down to 9.9 percent year on year from 31.0 percent in May 1996.
At the last central bank intervention on Wednesday the naira appreciated to 82 naira to the dollar from 83 a week before. It has not drifted far from the 85 mark for well over 18 months.

But the economy of Africa's most populous nation, largely dependent on crude oil exports, feels the pinch as soon as government spending stops. This year the finance ministry did not release its budgeted capital spending until the start of August.

Even when the money did reach the system the central bank mopped up the "excess" liquidity through increased sales of treasury bills out of fear that inflation could surge and the naira come under pressure.

"The measures have pushed lending rates to between 25 and 35 percent from 16 to 20 percent earlier this year, but nobody needs to borrow money anyway because there is no need to expand in a shrinking market," said Okeke.

Gloom greets the daily rush on the stock market to sell what were once considered safe investments in blue chip companies -- both because shareholders need the money and because they see prices falling further after a chain of poor corporate results.

Okeke said manufacturers were also being driven to breaking point by the decay of infrastructure and state-run utilities, which both the lack of spending and a reluctance to privatise have left in a woeful state.

"If you look just at power, then companies here in Lagos have had to use their own generators for at least 80 percent of this year and of course the small companies can't afford the extra cost and have to close up shop," said Okeke.
Fuel shortages, caused by breakdowns at state-run refineries paralysed business for months earlier in the year, making imports necessary and prompting calls for privatisation.

Business and the World Bank have pushed privatisation as a way of breaking the recession which has lasted since the political and economic crisis began in 1993 with an election annulment, but so far Abacha has appeared reluctant to heed their advice.

"Privatisation can be a long term solution to some of these problems, but in the short term if the government would spend on infrastructure it will not only improve business conditions but will stimulate demand," said Okeke.
